newsitem.title: UK: Japan liquidity threat to world markets seen muted.
newsitem.headline: Japan liquidity threat to world markets seen muted.

text.p: The threat to world financial markets from a large-scale repatriation of Japanese capital is overestimated, according to a study by HSBC James Capel.
It said one of the greatest fears of world financial markets was the prospect of a collapse in U.S. asset prices sparked by a reversal of the substantial Japanese inflows of recent years.

The concern was highlighted in late June when Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto rocked U.S. markets when he seemed to suggest that Japan might sell U.S. Treasuries if Washington did not cooperate with Tokyo to stabilise currencies.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said at the time he saw no reason to expect concerted sales of U.S. Treasury securities and voiced confidence U.S. markets could absorb them if they occurred.

The study said the dollar/yen rate was likely to be the most affected by a pressure for the reversal of Japanese inflows into U.S. markets. Any pressure was likely to lead to a sharp yen rise, thus choking off much of the repatriation.
HSBC James Capel international economist Don Smith argues that the fear is rooted in confusion about the connection between the weak Japanese economy and strong U.S. markets.
"The various theories that attempt to explain a link between these two phenomena do not stand up to close scrutiny," he said.
In particular, the idea that a pool of money emanating from Japan has somehow spilled over into world markets grossly misrepresents what has occurred."

While there is clear evidence of substantial Japanese inflows, much has come from the public sector and largely represents an attempt to prevent a sliding dollar leaving the yen uncompetitive during a period of extreme Japanese economic weakness.
"We expect that a reversal of this intervention to depress the dollar will not be required - at least not at anything like the extent of the intervention during the early 1990s," the study said.
Smith said a combination of weaker U.S. growth and an improvement in Japan's economic picture should weaken the dollar in the second half of the year.
He also said the role of the yen in choking off a sudden desire to repatriate funds had been underestimated.
"If the yen does its job properly, it should rise sharply to increase the attractiveness of U.S. assets and keep overall Japanese capital outflows in line with the current account surplus."

Even if there was a substantial repatriation of Japanese funds, he said the potential consequences for U.S. asset prices was overstated. For a start, Japanese inflows have mainly been to bonds, and the threat to equities is therefore indirect.
Also, despite substantial overseas inflows into the U.S. market, he said yields had not been artificially depressed.

"In the short term, a sizeable repatriation of Japanese funds from the U.S. bond market would almost certainly cause some short-term uncertainty and depress U.S. asset prices. But we suspect that any weakness is likely to be met with buying interest from elsewhere, given the fair value of the market," he said.
The study said the size of the yen rise would depend on the extent of the pressure for repatriation.

"Our central forecast is that the yen appreciate to 105 against the dollar by Q1 1998. However, in the event of a particularly strong recovery in the Japanese economy over the next 18 months, the yen could well appreciate below the 90 level," Smith said.
